title: After a head, how often is a head next?
hook: A fair coin, four flips. Look only at flips that follow a head. What share are heads?

knows: each flip of a fair coin is independent of the last (gamblers-fallacy)
doesNotKnow: that averaging a share within short sequences is biased below 50%
how this counting method misled hot-hand studies

misconception: In a fair coin sequence the average share of heads right after a heads is 50%, so any lower share is evidence the coin is cold after heads.
objective: The learner can say that averaging the per-sequence share over four-flip sequences gives 40.5%, while pooling all flips after a head gives exactly 50%, so the lower average comes from how it is counted.
keyState: All 14 four-flip sequences that have a flip after a head opened: shares average 17/42 = 40.5%; pooled 12 of 24 = 50%.

claims.text: Of the 16 sequences of four fair flips, 14 have at least one flip right after a head; TTTT and TTTH have none.
claims.source: Enumeration of all 16 sequences (SEQS in model.ts; recomputed in node).

claims.text: Averaging each sequence's share of heads after a head over those 14 sequences gives 17/42 = 40.5%.
claims.source: Sum of shares = 17/3 over 14 sequences = 17/42 = 0.4048 (avgShare(); the 14 shares are listed on the tiles).

claims.text: Pooling every flip that follows a head over all 16 sequences, 12 of 24 are heads: exactly 50%.
claims.source: Each of the three positions after the first has a head before it in 8 of the 16 sequences, giving 24 flips, and half of them (12) are heads; pooled() in model.ts.

claims.text: Each flip is still fair; the lower average comes from averaging per-sequence shares, because sequences with many heads in a row contribute many flips after a head but only one share.
claims.source: Follows from claims 2 and 3: the same flips give 40.5% by averaging shares and 50% by pooling.

claims.text: Miller and Sanjurjo (2018) showed that this counting bias affected early studies of the hot hand in basketball.
claims.source: Miller, J. B. & Sanjurjo, A. (2018). Surprised by the hot hand fallacy? A truth in the law of small numbers. Econometrica 86(6): 2019-2047. To be checked: wording of 'early studies'. The lesson makes no claim about whether the hot hand exists.

recall.question: You average, over many 4-flip fair-coin sequences, each sequence's share of heads right after a head. Roughly what do you get?
recall.why: Averaging shares within short sequences gives 40.5% for four flips, although pooling all flips after a head gives exactly 50%.
